title: Web App Boilerplate
description: React + Express starter. Get from zero to running code in 10 minutes.

learningObjectives.text: Set up a React frontend with Vite
Create an Express backend that serves API routes
Connect frontend to backend with fetch

contentSections.body: You could use Next.js, Remix, SvelteKit, or any of 50 other frameworks. But React + Vite + Express gives you the clearest separation between 'the thing users see' and 'the thing that calls Claude.' Once you understand this pattern, every framework makes sense.

### The architecture

```
Browser (React)  →  /api/chat  →  Express  →  Claude API
                 ←  response  ←           ←
```

**Why not call Claude directly from the browser?**
Your API key would be visible in the source code. Anyone could steal it and charge requests to your account.

**The backend is your gatekeeper:**
- Stores the API key securely (env variable)
- Validates user auth (later)
- Controls costs (rate limits, caps)

contentSections.question: What happens if you put your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in your React frontend code?
contentSections.answer: **Anyone can steal it.** React code is public — it's downloaded by every browser. Even if you obfuscate it, the key is visible in network requests. With your key, anyone can make API calls at your expense. Always keep secret keys on the server.
contentSections.hint: How does a browser run React code — on your server, or on the user's machine?

contentSections.body: Frontend = what users see. Backend = where secrets live. Never put API keys in frontend code.

contentSections.scenario: You put your Anthropic API key directly in your React frontend code so the browser can call Claude directly.
contentSections.question: What's wrong with this?

options.label: Nothing — it's simpler and works fine
The API key would be visible in the source code; anyone could steal it

feedback.exposed: Right — anyone could view your page source and steal the key, then charge requests to your account.
feedback.fine: It would technically work, but the API key becomes visible to anyone viewing your page's source — a real security hole.

contentSections.concept: The backend is your gatekeeper: stores the API key securely (env variable), validates user auth, controls costs (rate limits, caps). Browser → /api/chat → Express → Claude API — never browser → Claude directly.

contentSections.body: **Vite proxy:** Add to `vite.config.js` → `server: { proxy: { '/api': 'http://localhost:3001' }}`. Now `fetch('/api/chat')` hits your backend automatically in dev — no CORS issues.

title: Integrate Claude API
description: Connect your React frontend to Claude via Express. Add streaming for live output.

learningObjectives.text: Build an Express route that calls Claude and returns results
Implement streaming responses with Server-Sent Events
Handle errors from the API gracefully in the UI

contentSections.body: ChatGPT shows text appearing word by word. That's not magic — it's streaming. Without streaming, users wait 10 seconds for a blank screen, then see all the text at once. With streaming, they see progress immediately. That 10-second wait feels like 2 seconds.

contentSections.question: What HTTP content type does Server-Sent Events use?
contentSections.answer: **`text/event-stream`**. This special content type tells the browser to keep the connection open and parse incoming data as a stream of events. Each event is formatted as `data: [content]\n\n`. The browser's `EventSource` API handles parsing automatically.
contentSections.hint: SSE is a specific protocol. What header tells the browser it's receiving a stream?

contentSections.body: SSE = keep HTTP connection open, send `data: [text]\n\n` chunks. Frontend reads them with EventSource or fetch + ReadableStream.

contentSections.scenario: Without streaming, users wait 10 seconds for a blank screen, then see all the text at once. With streaming, that same 10-second wait feels like 2 seconds.
contentSections.question: Why does it feel faster if the total time is the same?

options.label: Streaming actually makes Claude generate faster
Seeing progress immediately changes perceived wait time, not actual generation time

feedback.perceived: Right — streaming sends each word as it's generated via SSE; the browser renders progressively. Generation time is unchanged; what changes is the user sees something happening right away instead of a blank screen.
feedback.faster-gen: Not accurate — the underlying generation time is unchanged. What changes is when the user starts seeing output.

contentSections.mechanism: Non-streaming: wait for the full response, return it as JSON. Streaming: send each word as it's generated using Server-Sent Events; the browser renders progressively. That's why a 10-second wait feels like 2 seconds, even though generation time didn't change.

title: Styling & UX
description: Make your tool look good. CSS, responsive design, interaction states.

learningObjectives.text: Apply basic CSS to make a tool look polished
Add loading states and error handling to UI
Design for small screens (mobile-first)

contentSections.body: You don't need to be a designer to ship a tool that looks professional. 80% of 'good design' is: good typography, enough whitespace, and consistent colors. The other 20% takes years to learn. Start with the 80%.

### The 5 rules that cover 80% of design

1. **Max width 680px** on content blocks — long lines are hard to read
2. **Generous padding** — `padding: 24px` feels like a product, `padding: 4px` feels like a test
3. **One font** — pick a system font stack or one Google Font
4. **Limit colors** — background, text, one accent (your brand color), one danger (red)
5. **Loading states** — always show *something* is happening

```css
.container { max-width: 680px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 24px; }
body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; background: #0f0f0f; color: #e8e8e8; }
.accent { color: #7fff7f; } /* one accent color */
```

contentSections.question: A user submits a form. The API call takes 8 seconds. What should the UI do?
contentSections.answer: **Show a loading state immediately.** Disable the submit button, show a spinner or 'Thinking...' text, and optionally stream the output as it arrives. An 8-second blank screen feels broken. An 8-second stream with text appearing feels fast.
contentSections.hint: Think about perceived performance vs. actual performance.

contentSections.body: Perceived performance > actual performance. A loading indicator makes 8 seconds feel like 3.

contentSections.scenario: You're styling a tool you just built and want to hit the 80% of good design that matters most.
contentSections.question: Which of these are part of the lesson's real 5 rules?

items.label: Max width ~680px on content blocks
Generous padding, not padding: 4px
One font — a system font stack or one Google Font
A limited palette — background, text, one accent, one danger color
Always show that something is happening (a loading state)
Mixing 3-4 different fonts to add visual interest
Full-width text blocks with no max-width constraint

explanation.max-width: Real rule — long lines are hard to read past ~680px.
explanation.padding: Real rule — padding: 24px feels like a product, padding: 4px feels like a test.
explanation.one-font: Real rule — one font, not several.
explanation.limit-colors: Real rule — background, text, one accent, one danger. That's it.
explanation.loading-states: Real rule — always show something is happening.
explanation.many-fonts: Not one of the rules — the rule is exactly the opposite: pick one font.
explanation.full-width: Not one of the rules — the rule is a max-width constraint, since long lines are hard to read.

contentSections.synthesis: 80% of good design is typography, whitespace, and consistent colors — five concrete rules, not artistic talent.

contentSections.body: **Copy before you design.** Write the actual text your UI will show ('What do you want to summarize?', 'Here's your result:', 'Something went wrong — try again'). Good copy makes average design feel polished.

title: Launch with Vercel
description: From local code to live on the internet in 2 minutes.

learningObjectives.text: Deploy a React app to Vercel
Configure environment variables for production
Set up a custom domain

contentSections.body: There's a specific kind of pride that comes from typing a URL and seeing something YOU built appear in a browser anywhere in the world. Vercel makes that happen in 2 minutes. No servers to manage. No infrastructure. Just push and it's live.

### The Vercel model

Vercel hosts:
1. **Static files** — your built React app (HTML, CSS, JS)
2. **Serverless functions** — your API routes (run on-demand, scale automatically)

For our Express backend, Vercel needs it in a specific format:
- Move your API routes to `/api/*.mjs` files
- Each file exports a default function `(req, res) => {}`
- Vercel detects these and deploys them as serverless functions

Or: deploy frontend on Vercel, backend on Railway/Render.

contentSections.question: What's a serverless function? Does it run on a server?
contentSections.answer: **Yes, it runs on a server — just not one you manage.** 'Serverless' means you don't provision or maintain servers. You write a function, Vercel runs it when called, charges per execution, and scales automatically. For infrequent API calls, this is dramatically cheaper than a dedicated server.
contentSections.hint: Think about the difference between 'I own this server' vs 'someone else runs code for me when needed.'

contentSections.body: Serverless = you write functions, the platform handles servers. Free tier handles thousands of requests/day.

### Option A: Vercel CLI (fastest)
```bash
npm install -g vercel
vercel login
vercel  # from your project root
```
Follow prompts. Your app is live in ~60 seconds.

### Option B: Git integration (best for ongoing projects)
1. Push your code to GitHub
2. Go to vercel.com → New Project → Import from GitHub
3. Vercel auto-detects React/Vite and configures build settings
4. Every push to `main` auto-deploys

### Add env variables in Vercel dashboard:
- Settings → Environment Variables
- Add: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = sk-ant-...`
- Never put this in your code or `.env` committed to git
**Never commit .env to git.** Add `.env` to `.gitignore` before your first commit. Once a secret is in git history, it's compromised — even if you delete it later.

contentSections.question: Put these Vercel CLI deployment steps in order.
steps: Run vercel from your project root
Your app is live in ~60 seconds
contentSections.explanation: You need the CLI installed before you can log in, and logged in before vercel from your project root can actually deploy anything under your account. Env variables like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY still get added separately in the dashboard — never committed to git.

contentSections.body:
### Add your domain

1. Vercel dashboard → your project → Settings → Domains
2. Add your domain (e.g., `pr-describe.tools`)
3. Vercel shows you the DNS records to set
4. In your domain registrar (Porkbun, Namecheap, etc.) → add those DNS records
5. Wait 5-30 minutes for DNS propagation

### Good domain options for tools:
- `.tools` TLD — descriptive, ~$20/year
- `.app` — professional, ~$15/year
- `yourdomain.com/tools/toolname` — if you already have a domain
- `toolname.vercel.app` — free, fine for sharing and testing

### After deploy, share:
- Tweet/post with a screenshot of the input/output
- Share in relevant Slack/Discord communities
- Add to your portfolio

title: Errors & Loading States
description: Claude takes 3 seconds to respond. Your UI needs to say something during those 3 seconds — and when things go wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a blank screen during an API call is a usability failure
Implement loading and error states in a React component that calls Claude
Write error messages that tell the user what to do next

contentSections.body: You click submit. Nothing happens for three seconds. Did it work? Is it stuck? Should you click again? Most web app bugs people report as 'it's broken' are actually just: nobody built a loading state, so the app looked frozen.

contentSections.question: Why disable the button while status is 'loading', instead of just showing a spinner next to it?
contentSections.answer: **To prevent duplicate submissions.** Without disabling it, an impatient click during the 3-second wait fires a second identical request — doubling your API cost and potentially showing two conflicting results. Disabling the trigger is as important as showing the loading indicator.
contentSections.hint: What happens if someone clicks the button twice while it's still loading?

contentSections.scenario: A fetch call fails with err.message containing "Failed to fetch".
contentSections.question: What should the user see?

options.label: 'Error.'
"Can't reach the server. Check your connection and try again."

feedback.specific: Right — map technical errors to specific, actionable sentences. 'Failed to fetch' means a network/connectivity issue, and the message should say so plainly.
feedback.generic: That's the bad-error-message pattern the lesson warns against — it tells the user nothing about what happened or what to do.

contentSections.concept: Bad: 'Error.' / 'Something went wrong.' / a raw stack trace. Good: tells the user what happened, in plain language, and what to do about it. Only fall back to a generic message when you genuinely don't know what happened — and even then, tell the user to retry.

contentSections.body: Every async action needs idle, loading, and success/error states — and the trigger should be disabled during loading, not just visually different.

**Never show a raw error object or stack trace to users.** It's unhelpful to non-technical users and can leak implementation details. Log the raw error to your monitoring tool; show the user a plain-language translation.

title: The boilerplate that's still one file too many
description: Trimming a fresh Next.js app to what it actually needs, and deciding what earns its own file on day one versus what can stay inline until it's used twice.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which parts of a scaffolded app are genuinely dead weight versus load-bearing
Decide what a new app's file structure should contain on day one, before any real feature exists

contentSections.body: You run `npx create-next-app@latest briefdesk` — briefdesk turns a client's rambling intake email into a structured project brief with Claude. Fifteen files appear: a `globals.css`, an `app/layout.tsx`, an `app/page.tsx` with a Next.js logo and a counter demo, an `eslint.config.mjs`, a `next.config.ts`, three placeholder SVGs in `public/`. None of it is briefdesk. All of it has to be looked at before you know what to delete.

contentSections.scenario: A fresh `create-next-app` scaffold includes: the default `app/page.tsx` demo content (logo, links to Next.js docs, a deploy button), the `app/layout.tsx` shell that wraps every page, `globals.css` with Tailwind's base imports, `next.config.ts`, and `public/vercel.svg` / `public/next.svg` / `public/file.svg`.
contentSections.question: Which of these is genuinely dead weight for briefdesk — safe to delete on day one — versus load-bearing scaffolding you'd keep even though it looks empty right now?

options.label: Delete the page.tsx demo content and the placeholder SVGs; keep layout.tsx, globals.css and next.config.ts even though they look nearly empty
Delete all of it and start layout.tsx and page.tsx from a blank file
Keep everything as-is — the demo content documents how routing works and might be useful reference later

feedback.delete-demo-keep-shell: Right. The demo content in page.tsx (logo, doc links, deploy button) is genuinely dead weight — it teaches nothing you don't already know and it's actively in the way of the real first screen. layout.tsx, globals.css and next.config.ts look empty but they're the actual plumbing: layout.tsx is where a global nav or a Claude-client provider will eventually live, globals.css is where Tailwind's imports live, next.config.ts is where you'll add image domains or env passthroughs later. Deleting those and rebuilding them from scratch wastes time re-discovering settings the scaffold already got right.
feedback.delete-everything: This throws away correctly-configured plumbing along with the disposable demo. layout.tsx's `<html>`/`<body>` structure and font setup, globals.css's Tailwind directives, and next.config.ts's defaults are all things you'd have to reconstruct from memory or docs — the scaffold already got them right, so rebuilding from a blank file is pure lost time for zero benefit.
feedback.keep-everything: The demo content isn't reference material — it's a Next.js logo and links to docs.nextjs.org that will never be relevant to briefdesk again. Keeping it doesn't preserve anything useful; it just means the first real screen has to be built around content that has to eventually be deleted anyway.

contentSections.concept: **A fresh scaffold has two layers: the plumbing (layout, global styles, config) that's genuinely load-bearing even when it looks nearly empty, and the demo content (a placeholder page, sample assets) that exists only to prove the scaffold works and should be deleted on day one, not kept as reference.**

contentSections.body:
Ten minutes with a fresh scaffold, before writing any feature: ``` briefdesk/ app/ layout.tsx # keep — global /, font, will hold providers later page.tsx # gut the demo content, leave a single

briefdesk

globals.css # keep — Tailwind's @tailwind directives next.config.ts # keep — defaults are fine until you need image domains etc. public/ vercel.svg # delete next.svg # delete file.svg # delete window.svg # delete ``` The rule for this pass is narrow on purpose: delete what's unambiguously demo content, touch nothing else. `app/page.tsx` becomes a single heading, not an empty file — an empty file with no content at all makes it harder to tell "this route intentionally renders nothing yet" from "this route was never wired up." Everything else — folder structure for components, a `lib/` directory, a Claude client wrapper — doesn't exist yet, because none of it is needed yet. The temptation at this exact moment is to also set up `components/`, `lib/`, `types/` because "you'll need them eventually" — the next lesson is about resisting that until the first real feature actually asks for it.
A fresh scaffold has load-bearing plumbing and disposable demo content — delete the demo on day one, and don't invent folders for a feature that doesn't exist yet.

contentSections.title: The folder that's still empty in month two

contentSections.body: A different team's briefdesk clone has `components/`, `hooks/`, `utils/`, `lib/`, `types/`, `constants/` and `services/` — created on day one, "because that's how a real app is structured." Two months and one real feature later, four of those seven folders have exactly one file in them, and two are still empty.

contentSections.scenario: A fresh Next.js scaffold for briefdesk has a `components/`, `hooks/`, `utils/`, `lib/`, `types/`, `constants/` and `services/` folder created on day one, before any feature beyond the single intake form exists.
contentSections.question: Of those 7 folders created up front, how many will actually contain a file by the time the app has its first two real features (the intake form, and a list of saved briefs)?
contentSections.unit: folders with at least one file
contentSections.explanation: Realistically about 3: `components/` (a `BriefForm` and a `BriefCard`), `lib/` (the Claude client wrapper), and maybe `types/` (a `Brief` type). `hooks/`, `utils/`, `constants/` and `services/` typically stay empty until the app is substantially bigger than two features — there's no custom hook yet, no util function used in two places yet, no service layer distinct from `lib/`. Four of the seven folders were a guess that hadn't paid off yet, and in the meantime every new file had to be placed against a taxonomy that didn't reflect the app's actual shape.

contentSections.body:
Folder structure is supposed to answer a question someone will actually ask: "where does X live?" A folder with zero or one file in it two months in isn't answering that question — it's a guess about a future that hasn't arrived, and it costs something real even while it's empty: every new file now has seven plausible homes instead of one obvious one, and a new contributor has to learn a taxonomy that doesn't yet reflect anything in the app.

The alternative that scales down to a one-feature app and up to a real one: start with everything Next.js's App Router already gives you a place for — `app/` for routes, colocated `page.tsx` files — and add exactly one new top-level folder the moment something needs it, not before:

```
briefdesk/
  app/
    page.tsx          # the one screen that exists
    layout.tsx
```

That's the whole structure worth having until a second screen, a shared component, or a piece of logic used in two places actually shows up. `lib/`, `components/`, `types/` get created the day their first real file exists, not the day the project does.

Create a folder the day its first real file exists, not the day the project does — an empty folder isn't neutral, it's a guess about a future that might not arrive, and it adds a decision every new file now has to make.

title: Components, and when a page is not yet one
description: Deciding when a chunk of JSX earns its own component versus staying inline, and what a good extraction actually removes versus what it just relocates.

learningObjectives.text: Decide whether a piece of JSX should become its own component based on reuse and independent meaning, not size
Extract a component with a props interface that hides its internals instead of just moving code to a new file

contentSections.title: Long isn't the same problem as tangled

contentSections.body: `app/page.tsx` is 180 lines: a form with four fields, a submit handler that calls `/api/briefs`, a loading spinner, an error banner, and — once briefs start coming back — a list of saved briefs rendered below the form. A teammate opens it and says "this needs to be broken into components, it's huge." Is the length actually the problem?

contentSections.question: The file is long, but is it structurally tangled? What's the actual signal that something here is worth extracting into its own component?

options.label: The line count alone (180 lines) is the signal — anything over roughly 100-150 lines should be split
The `<li>` rendering a single brief is a self-contained, independently meaningful unit — worth extracting because it has its own clear identity (a BriefCard), not because of the file's length
Nothing here is worth extracting yet — one file with one form and one list is still simple enough to read top to bottom

feedback.length-alone: Line count is a lagging indicator, not a cause — a 180-line file that's one linear, easy-to-follow story (form, then list, then done) can be perfectly readable, while a 60-line file with three unrelated concerns tangled together can be genuinely hard to follow. The number itself doesn't tell you where the seam is.
feedback.brief-item-reuse: Right. The `<li>` block rendering a single brief — title, summary, deliverable count — is a self-contained unit with its own clear identity: it takes one `Brief` and renders it, independent of the form or the fetch logic around it. That independence, not the file's overall length, is what makes it a good extraction candidate. It'll also be needed again the moment there's a `/briefs/[id]` detail page or a dashboard card — reuse that's already visible, not merely hypothetical.
feedback.nothing-yet: The form-and-list combination is readable today, but the `<li>` block specifically already has an independent identity distinct from the page around it — a `Brief` in, JSX out, no dependency on the form's state. Extracting doesn't require it to feel painful yet; it requires the boundary to already be real, and here it is.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The extraction that actually helps here is a `<BriefCard brief={b} />` component taking one `Brief` and rendering it — nothing else in the file has that same self-contained shape yet. The form and the fetch logic are still one coherent story about "submitting client notes" and don't yet have a second, independent identity pulling on them.

contentSections.body: Extract a component when a chunk of JSX has an identity independent of what's around it, not when a file crosses some line count — length is a symptom you notice, not the actual test.

contentSections.title: An extraction that only moved the problem

contentSections.body: A teammate "fixes" the long page.tsx by pulling everything into a `<PageContent />` component that takes the same six props and thirty lines it always had, just in a different file now imported into a nearly-empty page.tsx. The diff looks like progress. Nothing got simpler.

contentSections.scenario: `page.tsx` shrinks from 180 lines to 8 — it now just renders `<PageContent />`. `PageContent.tsx` is 172 lines, containing the exact same form, state, fetch call and list rendering as before, just moved wholesale into a new file with a new name.
contentSections.question: Why doesn't this refactor actually reduce complexity, even though `page.tsx` is now dramatically shorter?

options.label: PageContent is a bad name — a more descriptive name would have fixed it
Nothing was decomposed — the same tangle of concerns (form state, fetch logic, list rendering) just moved to a different file wholesale, with an import added
The refactor is fine — a shorter page.tsx is strictly better regardless of what PageContent contains

feedback.wrong-file-name: The name isn't the issue — even a perfectly named `PageContent` component still contains the form, the fetch logic, and the list rendering all tangled together exactly as before. Renaming the container doesn't separate the concerns living inside it.
feedback.moved-not-decomposed: Right. A real extraction identifies an independent unit (like the BriefCard from the previous section) and gives it its own boundary — a props interface that hides what's inside. This move did neither: it took the entire undivided tangle and relocated it, so anyone reading PageContent.tsx has to hold the exact same six concerns in their head at once, just one file removed from where they started.
feedback.should-stay-inline: A shorter page.tsx sounds like progress but isn't the actual goal — the goal is fewer things to hold in your head at once when reading or changing code. This refactor makes page.tsx shorter while leaving PageContent.tsx exactly as tangled as the original was, so nothing about the app actually got easier to reason about.

contentSections.mechanism: Complexity moved, not removed: the file boundary changed but the same six concerns (form fields, submit state, the fetch call, error display, the brief list, and BriefCard rendering) are still one undifferentiated block, just under a different filename with an extra import to follow. A real decomposition would pull `BriefCard` out with its own props (as in the previous section), extract the submit logic into a `useBriefSubmit` hook or similar once it's genuinely reused, and leave page.tsx composing clearly-named, independently-understandable pieces — not one big piece wearing a new name.

contentSections.body: The test for whether an extraction actually helped: could you describe the new component in one sentence that doesn't just restate "it's the page"? `BriefCard` passes — "renders one brief." `PageContent` doesn't — its one-sentence description is still "the whole page, minus the outer wrapper," which is exactly what it was before the move. A component earns its name when the name tells you what it does without needing to open the file; a component that's just a renamed container for everything that used to be there hasn't earned anything yet, and the codebase now has one more file to open to find out what it actually contains.

Moving a whole tangle of concerns to a new file with a new name isn't decomposition — a real extraction gives one independent unit its own boundary, and you should be able to describe it in a sentence that isn't just 'the rest of the page.'

title: State: local, shared, and the difference that matters
description: Keeping state where it's used until two components genuinely need the same value at the same time, and lifting it to the nearest common ancestor instead of reaching for global state early.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a stale-UI bug caused by duplicated state instead of shared state
Lift state to the nearest common ancestor component rather than introducing global state prematurely

contentSections.title: Two components, two copies of the truth

contentSections.body: briefdesk grows a header showing "3 briefs this week" next to the main list. Someone generates a new brief, the list updates immediately — the count next to it still says 3, not 4, until the page is refreshed. Nothing crashed. Nothing logged an error. The number is just wrong.

contentSections.scenario: `<BriefList />` fetches briefs and keeps them in its own `useState`. `<WeeklyCount />`, rendered next to it in the header, independently fetches the same briefs endpoint and keeps its own separate `useState` to compute a count. Generating a new brief updates BriefList's local state (it's the component handling the submit) but WeeklyCount never re-fetches — it only fetched once, on mount.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind the stale count, and what does it reveal about how the state was structured?

options.label: A flaky network request that intermittently failed to update WeeklyCount
The same underlying data (the list of briefs) exists as two independent copies of state, in two components, with no mechanism keeping them in sync
A React rendering bug where sibling components don't re-render together

feedback.network-flake: The fetch itself isn't failing — WeeklyCount's fetch worked fine on mount and produced a correct count at that moment. The bug is that nothing tells it to fetch again when the underlying data changes, because as far as WeeklyCount knows, its one copy of the data is still current.
feedback.duplicated-state: Right. There's exactly one real fact — the current list of briefs — and it's living in two separate useState calls with no relationship to each other. BriefList's copy gets updated when a submit happens because that's the component doing the submitting; WeeklyCount's copy has no way to find out that happened, because it's not the same state, just two states that started out equal.
feedback.react-bug: React re-renders exactly what you tell it to, based on the state you gave it. Nothing about sibling components is special here — both would re-render correctly if their state actually changed. The problem is upstream of rendering: WeeklyCount's state was never told to change.

contentSections.mechanism: **When two components each hold their own copy of what's conceptually the same data, nothing automatically keeps those copies equal — an update to one copy has no way to reach the other.** The count wasn't wrong because of a bug in the count logic; it was wrong because there were two sources of truth for one fact, and only one of them got the memo.

contentSections.body: A stale-UI bug where one component doesn't see another's update is usually two copies of the same fact living in two separate useState calls — lift the state to their nearest common ancestor so there's exactly one copy.

contentSections.title: Not every shared value needs a context provider

contentSections.body: Fixing the stale count, a teammate reaches for React Context: a `BriefsProvider` wrapping the whole app, a `useBriefs()` hook, the works — for two sibling components three levels deep in one page. It's not wrong exactly. It's a lot of new machinery for a problem that props already solved.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk now has: (1) the briefs array, needed by BriefList and WeeklyCount, both rendered directly inside the same page; (2) the currently-selected brief on the detail page, needed by three components all nested inside that one page; (3) the logged-in user's name, needed by the header, the footer, and a settings page, none of which are anywhere near each other in the tree; (4) a single form's "is submitting" boolean, needed only by that form's own submit button.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually justify reaching for Context (or a similar app-wide mechanism) instead of just lifting state and passing props? Select all that apply.

items.label: The briefs array (case 1) — two siblings under one common, nearby parent
The selected brief (case 2) — three components nested inside one page
The logged-in user's name (case 3) — needed in places with no nearby common ancestor, effectively everywhere
The submit-in-progress boolean (case 4) — used only inside the one form that owns it

explanation.briefs-array: This is exactly the case from the first section — a nearby common ancestor (the page) already exists, and passing props two levels down costs nothing. Context here would add a provider, a hook, and a layer of indirection to solve a problem two lines of prop-passing already solves.
explanation.selected-brief: Same shape as the briefs array — everything that needs it is nested inside one page that can hold the state and pass it down. "Three components" sounds like a lot until you notice they're all close together in the same subtree.
explanation.user-name: This is the real case for Context — a value needed in the header, the footer, and a settings page has no single nearby ancestor that isn't the entire app, and threading it through every layer as props ("prop drilling") when most of those layers don't otherwise care about it is exactly the pain Context exists to remove.
explanation.submitting-flag: This value is used by exactly one component — its own submit button. It doesn't even need to be lifted, let alone put in Context; it's about as local as state gets.

contentSections.synthesis: The deciding question isn't "is this used by more than one component" — it's "how far apart are the components that need it, and would passing it as props mean threading it through several layers that don't otherwise care about it." Nearby siblings: lift state to their common parent. Genuinely everywhere, with no useful common ancestor: that's what Context is actually for.

contentSections.body: Lift state to the nearest common ancestor and pass it as props by default — reach for Context only when the components sharing a value have no useful common ancestor, not whenever more than one component needs something.

title: Routing for a tool with more than one screen
description: Deciding when a piece of UI earns its own route versus staying a conditional view on the same page, using the App Router's file-based conventions.

learningObjectives.text: Decide whether a new screen should be its own route or a conditional view within an existing one
Structure a multi-screen app using the App Router's file-based routing conventions

contentSections.title: A tab that should have been a URL

contentSections.body: briefdesk grows a detail view: clicking a brief in the list swaps the page's content to show that brief's full deliverables and timeline, toggled by a `selectedBrief` state variable. It works — until someone tries to bookmark a specific brief, or share a link to it with a client, and there's nothing to link to. Every brief lives at the same URL.

contentSections.scenario: Two pieces of UI in briefdesk: (1) a brief's detail view — title, full notes, deliverables, timeline — currently shown by conditionally rendering different JSX based on a `selectedBrief` state variable; (2) a small dropdown that toggles between showing deliverables sorted by date versus sorted by priority, within that same detail view.
contentSections.question: Which of these two genuinely needs its own route, and which is fine staying as conditional state on the same page?

options.label: The brief detail view should be its own route (/briefs/[id]); the sort toggle should stay as local state
Both deserve their own routes, for consistency
Neither needs a route — conditional rendering works fine for both and keeps things simpler

feedback.detail-yes-sort-no: Right. The test is whether a specific state is something a user would want to bookmark, share, reload into, or navigate to directly with the browser's back button. A specific brief's detail view passes that test clearly — someone should be able to send a client a link straight to their brief. The sort order of a list within that view fails it — nobody bookmarks 'deliverables sorted by priority,' and making it a route would mean a URL change on every dropdown click, which is worse UX, not more consistent.
feedback.both-routes: Consistency for its own sake isn't the test here — a route for the sort toggle would mean the URL changes every time someone clicks a dropdown, and reloading or sharing that URL wouldn't provide any value nobody's actually asking for. Not everything that changes what's on screen deserves a URL.
feedback.neither-routes: The detail view specifically fails this test in a way that matters: a brief without its own URL can't be bookmarked, shared with a client, or opened directly from a link — real things briefdesk's actual users would want to do with a specific brief. Keeping the sort toggle as state avoids adding a route for something nobody needs a URL for.

contentSections.concept: **A screen earns its own route when a user would plausibly want to bookmark it, share a link to it, or navigate straight to it — not merely because it's a distinct visual state.** A toggle, a sort order, or a filter that's fine to lose on reload should usually stay as component state, not a URL.

contentSections.body: A screen earns its own route when someone would plausibly want to bookmark, share, or navigate directly to that exact state — not every visual change deserves a URL, even in a multi-screen app.

briefdesk's `/briefs/[id]` page grows a second responsibility almost by accident: a query param, `/briefs/123?edit=true`, switches the same page from viewing a brief to editing it — same route, a conditional flag deciding which of two genuinely different screens renders.

contentSections.question: Viewing and editing a brief are both working here. What's the actual cost of handling them as one route with a query-param switch, rather than as two separate routes?

options.label: No real cost — both screens render correctly and the code is short
The route file now has two unrelated jobs (viewing, editing) bundled behind one condition, and neither one gets its own loading/error boundary, its own layout, or a URL that says what it actually is
searchParams shouldn't be used for anything except pagination

feedback.no-cost: It renders correctly today, at this size — the cost shows up as the two screens diverge. An edit form typically needs different loading behavior (a form pre-filled from data that might still be loading), different error handling (a save failure versus a fetch failure), and often a different layout. Bundling them behind one condition means every one of those differences has to be threaded through the same file with more conditions, instead of two files that can each stay simple.
feedback.conflated-concerns: Right. Next.js's file-based routing gives a route its own `loading.tsx` and `error.tsx` boundaries and its own layout for free — but only per route. One file doing two jobs behind a query-param switch can't take advantage of that; both the view and the edit experience have to share whatever loading and error handling gets written into this one file, and the URL itself (`/briefs/123?edit=true`) doesn't obviously say 'this is the edit screen' the way `/briefs/123/edit` would.
feedback.search-params-wrong: searchParams isn't misused mechanically — it's a legitimate way to read a query string. The problem isn't the tool, it's using it to switch between two screens that have different enough needs (loading states, error handling, layout) to deserve being two separate routes instead.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix follows the App Router's own convention for exactly this shape — a second `page.tsx` under an `edit/` subfolder: `app/briefs/[id]/page.tsx` for viewing, `app/briefs/[id]/edit/page.tsx` for editing. Each gets its own loading and error boundaries automatically, the URL (`/briefs/123/edit`) says what it is without needing to inspect a query param, and the view page stops needing to know editing exists at all.

contentSections.body:
```
app/
  briefs/
    [id]/
      page.tsx           # /briefs/123        — view
      loading.tsx          # loading state, view only
      edit/
        page.tsx           # /briefs/123/edit   — edit
        loading.tsx          # loading state, edit only
```

The App Router's file convention rewards giving each genuinely distinct screen its own route: `loading.tsx` and `error.tsx` are picked up automatically per-folder, so the edit screen's loading state (a form that might take a moment to populate) never has to share logic with the view screen's. This is the same instinct as the CLI-design module's subcommands-versus-flags question, aimed at routes instead of a terminal: once two things are different enough jobs, giving each its own boundary — a subcommand there, a route here — beats one entry point branching on a flag.
Two genuinely different screens — different loading behavior, different error handling, different layout needs — are usually worth two routes, not one route switching on a query param.

title: Refactoring before the third similar feature, not after
description: Timing an abstraction to the third occurrence of a pattern, so it's built from real, known variation instead of a guess about what future cases might need.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether two similar pieces of code should be abstracted now or left duplicated until a third case appears
Design an abstraction from three known, real cases rather than a guess about future variation

contentSections.title: The abstraction built for a future that didn't arrive

contentSections.body: briefdesk has one brief type so far — a general project brief. Before a second type exists, someone builds a generic `<BriefTypeRenderer config={briefTypeConfig} />` with a config object describing field layouts, so "adding a new brief type later is just a config change." The config shape is a guess. Nobody has seen a second brief type yet.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk currently has exactly one kind of brief. A teammate proposes building a generic, config-driven `BriefTypeRenderer` now, designed to handle any future brief type through configuration rather than code.
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with building this abstraction now, before a second brief type exists? Select all that apply.

items.label: The config shape is a guess about what future brief types will need to vary, made with zero real examples to check it against
Every future brief type now has to be expressed as data fitting a config schema, instead of straightforward code, even if the schema doesn't fit its actual needs
If the guessed config shape turns out wrong for the second real brief type, that's now a breaking change to the abstraction plus a new feature at the same time, instead of just a new feature
You can't build a config system at all with only one example to generalize from — this is a category error, not a timing problem

explanation.config-shape-guess: This is the core problem — a config schema is a claim about which parts of a brief type vary and which stay fixed, and with one example, there's no way to know that yet. It's not that generalizing from one example is impossible, it's that whatever shape gets picked is unverified.
explanation.extra-indirection: Once the config-driven renderer exists, even simple future changes have to route through its schema — if the schema's field types don't cover something a new brief type genuinely needs, someone now has to extend the abstraction itself to add a feature, rather than just writing the feature.
explanation.harder-to-change: This is the compounding cost: the second brief type doesn't just need to be built, it needs to be built in a way that either fits an unverified schema or forces a change to that schema — two entangled problems where 'just add the second brief type in code' would have been one simple one.
explanation.one-type-cant-generalize: It's not literally impossible to write config-driven code with one example — people do it, and sometimes get lucky. The actual objection isn't that it can't be done, it's that doing it this early means every one of the above costs is being paid for a guess, not a verified pattern.

contentSections.synthesis: None of this means abstraction is bad — it means abstracting from one example is abstracting from a guess. The fix isn't 'never build a config system,' it's waiting for enough real cases to know what the config actually needs to express.

contentSections.body: Duplication between two real cases is honest and cheap to live with — an abstraction built from one case, or zero, is a guess wearing the shape of a decision.

contentSections.title: What the third case actually reveals

contentSections.body: A third brief type arrives — a website-redesign brief. Now there are three `*BriefView` components, and the shared shape between them is finally visible: every one has a title, a labeled `<Section>` list of some kind, and a second labeled section. The genuinely different part, in every case, was just what the sections were called and what they contained.

contentSections.intro: With three real brief-type views in hand — ProjectBriefView, LogoBriefView, and now WebsiteBriefView — it's time to extract the pattern they actually share, built from what's genuinely common across all three rather than a guess.

fields.prompt: Looking at all three real components, what's the part that's genuinely different in every case, and needs to stay flexible in the abstraction?

options.label: The <h1> title rendering
The section labels and what content goes in each section
The outer <article> wrapper

feedback.sections: Right — every component wraps its content in the same <article><h1> shell, but the section labels ('Deliverables' vs 'Style references') and their content are different every time. That's the part a shared abstraction needs to take as a parameter, not hardcode.
feedback.titles:
The title rendering (

{brief.title}

) is actually identical across all three — it's part of what's shared, not what varies.
feedback.article-wrapper: The <article> wrapper is identical in all three components too — also part of the shared shell, not the varying part.

fields.prompt: What's identical across all three real components, and belongs in the shared shell rather than being re-specified for every brief type?

options.label: The <article> wrapper and the <h1>{brief.title} rendering
Nothing — every part differs enough to need its own configuration
Everything, including the section content — brief types should share one hardcoded layout

feedback.article-and-title: Right — this is exactly what the three real implementations show in common, verified by actually looking at three cases instead of guessing at one.
feedback.nothing: This contradicts what the three real components actually show — the <article> wrapper and the title rendering are byte-for-byte identical in all three, which is precisely the kind of genuine, verified commonality the rule of three is meant to surface.
feedback.everything: The section content is exactly the part that's different in every one of the three real cases — hardcoding it would mean the shared component couldn't actually render any of the three brief types correctly.

contentSections.body: The third real occurrence of a pattern is what tells you which parts are genuinely shared and which only looked shared with two data points — that's the moment to abstract, built from evidence instead of a guess.

title: Restructure seven tangled app layouts
description: Seven drills applying the module's filters — trimming boilerplate, extraction timing, state placement, route boundaries, and the rule of three — to app structures you haven't seen before.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's structural filters to unfamiliar app layouts at speed
Identify the specific structural mistake in a real snippet, not just that something feels disorganized

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing here expires — do them in one sitting or spread across a few.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Restructure a working prototype for growth
description: Take a real, working single-file prototype, trim it to what it needs, extract its first honest component, place its state correctly, and add a second feature timed against the first to prove the restructure actually paid off.

learningObjectives.text: Restructure an existing single-file app using this module's extraction and state-placement rules
Measure whether a restructure actually reduced the cost of adding a new, similar feature

contentSections.body: Every filter in this module — trimmed boilerplate, extraction timed to real independence, state kept as local as it can be, routes earning their URL, abstraction timed to the third case — is easiest to prove on a real prototype, not a hypothetical one. This lab restructures a working single-file app of your own (briefdesk-shaped or otherwise) and then times whether the restructure actually made the next feature faster to add.

contentSections.title: Restructure your prototype, then prove it
contentSections.brief: Start from a real, working prototype you have — a single `page.tsx` (or close to it) that does one thing end to end, the way briefdesk's first draft crammed a form, a fetch call, and a list into 180 lines. You're not adding features yet. You're restructuring what exists using this module's rules, then adding one new, similar feature and timing it against how long the first one took, to check whether the restructure actually paid for itself.
contentSections.deliverable: A restructured app with a second feature added faster than the first

stages.title: Audit and trim
stages.instructions: List what's currently in your prototype's main file. Mark anything that's leftover scaffolding (unused demo content, an empty folder created 'for later') and delete it. Note, honestly, how long your very first feature took to build in its original tangled form — you'll compare against this at the end.
stages.checkpoint: Scaffolding is trimmed, and you have an honest baseline time for the first feature.

stages.title: Extract one real component
stages.instructions: Find one chunk of JSX in your prototype with an identity independent of what's around it — the BriefCard test from this module's second lesson. Extract it into its own component with a typed props interface that hides its internals. If nothing in your app has that independent identity yet, extract the smallest thing that does, even a single repeated element.
stages.checkpoint: One component exists with a props interface, and you can describe what it does in one sentence that isn't 'the rest of the page.'

stages.title: Place the state correctly
stages.instructions: Identify any state in your app that's used by more than one component. For each, decide: does it belong lifted to a nearby common ancestor (the default), or is there a genuine case — no nearby common ancestor, needed in unrelated far-apart places — for something like Context? Fix any duplicated state you find (the WeeklyCount bug pattern from this module).
stages.checkpoint: Every piece of shared state has exactly one source of truth, placed at the right level, with a one-sentence justification for why it's there.

stages.title: Add a second feature and time it
stages.instructions: Add one new feature that's genuinely similar in shape to your first one (a second form, a second list view, a second brief type — whatever fits your app). Time how long it actually takes. Compare honestly against your baseline from stage 1: faster, the same, or slower — and if it wasn't faster, name the specific thing in your restructure that didn't pay off.
stages.checkpoint: A second feature exists, its build time is recorded, and you have an honest one-sentence verdict on whether the restructure paid for itself.

rubric.meets: No leftover demo content or empty folders remain; anything kept is load-bearing and you can say what it's for.

rubric.criterion: The extracted component has a real, independent identity
rubric.meets: The component can be described in one sentence that isn't a restatement of 'the rest of the page,' and its props interface hides its internals.

rubric.criterion: Shared state has exactly one source of truth
rubric.meets: No two components hold separate copies of the same fact; anything using Context has a stated reason a nearby common ancestor wasn't available.
Anything given its own route is something a user would plausibly bookmark, share, or navigate to directly — not just a distinct visual state.

rubric.criterion: The second feature is measurably faster or the gap is explained
rubric.meets: A real time comparison exists against the baseline, and if it wasn't faster, a specific, honest reason is named rather than glossed over.

contentSections.body: The real test of a restructure isn't whether the code looks tidier — it's whether the next similar feature was actually faster to add, and you should be able to say by how much.

title: Checkpoint — Structuring a Web App That Grows
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the last module of the CLI Tools phase, two from further back. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Structuring a Web App That Grows

questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: A fresh Next.js scaffold has a Next.js-logo demo page, and an also nearly-empty next.config.ts. What's the right move for each on day one?

options.label: Delete the demo content; keep next.config.ts even though it looks nearly empty — it's load-bearing plumbing
Delete both — an empty-looking config file is safe to remove and rebuild later
Keep both — the demo content is useful reference for how routing works

questions.explanation: The demo content is disposable; the config file only looks empty because its defaults haven't needed changing yet — it's already doing its job.

questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: What's the actual signal that a chunk of JSX is worth extracting into its own component?

options.label: It has an identity independent of what's around it — you could describe it in a sentence that isn't 'the rest of the page'
The containing file has crossed roughly 150 lines
It's been copy-pasted at least once already

questions.explanation: Length is a lagging symptom, not the test. A `PageContent` component that's just the whole tangle relocated to a new file fails this test even though it did shrink the original file.

questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: Two sibling components three lines apart in the same file both need the same array of briefs. What's the right fix, and when would Context actually be the right call instead?

options.label: Lift the state to their nearby common ancestor and pass it as props; reach for Context only when there's no useful nearby common ancestor at all
Always use Context for anything shared by more than one component
Each component should keep fetching and storing its own copy — that's simpler than coordinating

questions.explanation: This is the WeeklyCount bug from the module: two copies of the same fact with nothing keeping them in sync. Lifting state to a nearby ancestor fixes it without needing Context's machinery at all.

questions.from: This module — Structuring a Web App That Grows
questions.prompt: What's the deciding question for whether a screen should get its own route versus staying a conditional view on the same page?

options.label: Would a user plausibly want to bookmark, share, or navigate directly to that exact state?
Is the screen visually different enough from the current one?
Does the screen take more than one API call to render?

questions.explanation: A brief's detail view passes this test — someone should be able to send a client a direct link. A sort-order toggle fails it; nobody bookmarks a specific sort order.

questions.from: Previous module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: Where should an AI call be placed relative to a CLI tool's fast, frequently-run default path?

options.label: Behind an explicit flag or subcommand a user reaches for on purpose, kept off the fast default path
On the default path, so users get the benefit automatically without needing to know a flag exists
It doesn't matter as long as the call eventually completes

questions.explanation: A fast, constant command has no room in its latency budget for a network call; a slow, occasional one might. The decision is per-command, based on that command's existing frequency and speed.

questions.from: Previous module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: Why does caching an AI response by a hash of the input and the prompt version work better than manual cache invalidation?

options.label: A real change to either one naturally produces a different hash, invalidating the cache automatically instead of requiring someone to remember to clear it
Hashing makes the cache lookup faster than a plain key would
It isn't actually better — manual invalidation is more reliable

questions.explanation: The hash-based key means a stale cache entry is structurally impossible for a changed input or prompt — there's nothing to remember to invalidate.

questions.from: Previous module — Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
questions.prompt: A batch AI operation is about to process hundreds of items at real cost. What pattern does this deserve, per the module on keeping cost predictable?

options.label: A confirm-by-default, --yes-to-bypass prompt showing the estimated cost before it's spent — same pattern as any other consequential action
No special handling — the API's own rate limits will catch anything excessive
A hard cap that silently truncates the batch once a cost threshold is hit

questions.explanation: The module treats a large predictable spend the same as any other destructive or consequential action: show the cost, confirm by default, let --yes skip it deliberately.

questions.from: Older module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: Why does a raw stack trace fail as an error message, even though it technically contains the information about what went wrong?

options.label: It doesn't state what happened, why, or what to do next in language the person reading it can act on
Stack traces are always factually wrong about the actual cause
Nothing is wrong with a stack trace as the default error view

questions.explanation: A good error message answers what happened, why, and what to do next — a stack trace answers none of those for the person actually reading it, even when it's technically accurate.

questions.from: Older module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: A batch job catches every error internally so it never crashes. Why might it still be wrong to exit 0 at the end?

options.label: Surviving a failure and succeeding are different claims — if anything in the batch actually failed, the exit code needs to say so
It's not wrong — catching every error and exiting 0 is always the correct behavior for a batch job
Exit codes only matter for interactive commands, not batch jobs

questions.explanation: A caller checking the exit code needs to know whether the batch actually succeeded, not just that the process didn't crash — those are different facts.

questions.from: Older module — Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
questions.prompt: Why does a unit test of an internal function fail to exercise the same things a real CLI invocation does?

options.label: It never touches argument parsing, exit codes, or stdout/stderr routing — the exact three things a script calling the CLI actually depends on
Unit tests are strictly worse than integration tests in every situation
It's not actually different — a unit test covers everything a real invocation does

questions.explanation: Testing a CLI by spawning the real binary and asserting on stdout, stderr, and exit code separately is the only way to exercise the argument-parsing and exit-code wiring a plain unit test skips entirely.

title: Why the API key can never reach the browser
description: Understanding exactly how an API key leaks from client-side code even when it isn't printed to the console, and what a route handler buys that direct client-side calls can't.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the specific mechanism by which a client-side API key becomes visible to any visitor
Distinguish what a server-side route handler protects from what an environment variable alone protects

contentSections.title: The key that was never logged and still leaked

contentSections.body: briefdesk's first proof-of-concept calls Claude directly from a client component, using `NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. The developer is careful — nothing is `console.log`'d, the key never appears in a commit, there's no obvious leak in the code review. Three days after a soft launch, the Anthropic usage dashboard shows four times the expected spend.

contentSections.scenario: The key is stored in an environment variable prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_`, which Next.js is documented to inline into the client-side JavaScript bundle at build time — by design, for values genuinely meant to be public, like an analytics ID.
contentSections.question: Given nobody logged the key anywhere, how did it end up exposed?

options.label: The GitHub repository containing the code must have been compromised
The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix causes Next.js to inline the value directly into the JavaScript bundle every browser downloads — anyone can read it from the built files, no logging required
Someone on the same network as a user intercepted the request and read the key from network traffic

feedback.compromised-repo: No breach is needed — the key was never a secret in the deployed app to begin with. NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are meant to be embedded in client code by design; the mistake was using that mechanism for something that needed to stay private.
feedback.public-prefix-bundled: Right. NEXT_PUBLIC_ is Next.js's explicit, documented signal that a value should be inlined into the JavaScript every browser downloads — it exists for genuinely public values like an analytics tracking ID. Using it for a secret means the secret is sitting in plain text in the built bundle, readable by opening browser devtools and searching the source, no logging or breach required.
feedback.network-sniffing: HTTPS already protects data in transit between the browser and Anthropic's API — that's not where this leak happened. The key was visible before any request was even sent, sitting in the static JavaScript file the browser downloaded to load the page at all.

contentSections.mechanism: **A `NEXT_PUBLIC_`-prefixed (or any client-bundled) environment variable isn't hidden by not being logged — it's compiled directly into the JavaScript source every visitor's browser downloads, and reading it requires nothing more than opening devtools' Sources tab.** The mistake wasn't a leak in the traditional sense; it was using the public-value mechanism for a value that was never supposed to be public.

contentSections.body: A NEXT_PUBLIC_-prefixed key isn't leaked by a mistake in logging — it's compiled straight into the browser bundle by design. The fix is a plain env var read only by server-side code the browser never receives.

contentSections.title: What the server actually adds, beyond hiding the key

contentSections.body: "We moved the key server-side" sounds like the whole fix. It buys more than that — a route handler is also the only place briefdesk can validate what's being sent to Claude, cap how much a single request can cost, or stop a request before it happens at all. None of that is possible when the browser talks to Claude directly.

contentSections.scenario: With the key safely server-side, briefdesk's /api/brief route now sits between the browser and Claude. Consider what that position actually enables.
contentSections.question: Which of these does moving the call server-side genuinely enable, beyond just hiding the API key? Select all that apply.

items.label: Rejecting a request before it reaches Claude if clientNotes is empty or absurdly large
Enforcing a fixed max_tokens ceiling regardless of what a modified client sends
Limiting how many requests a single user can make per minute, something a browser-only setup has no way to enforce
Guaranteeing Claude's output is always factually correct
Making the underlying model itself respond faster

explanation.validate-input: A route handler is a real checkpoint — it can look at the request and simply not call Claude at all if the input is obviously malformed or empty, something impossible to enforce from a browser that talks directly to Anthropic.
explanation.cap-tokens: Because the server constructs the actual API call, it controls max_tokens regardless of what a browser sends — a modified or malicious client can't override a limit it never gets to set in the first place.
explanation.rate-limit: Rate limiting (this module's last lesson) is only possible from a position that sees every request — a browser calling Claude directly has no shared, trustworthy place to count requests across users; the server does.
explanation.guarantee-quality: Nothing about server-side placement changes what the model itself produces — moving the call doesn't touch Claude's actual output quality or correctness, which is a separate concern this module doesn't claim to solve.
explanation.speed-up-model: The route handler adds a network hop, if anything — it doesn't make the model faster. Its value is control and safety, not raw speed.

contentSections.synthesis: Hiding the key is the reason a server-side call is non-negotiable, but it isn't the only thing the server-side position buys — it's also the only place any of this module's later lessons (streaming, retries, rate limiting) are even possible to build.

contentSections.body: This reframes the rest of the module: every lesson from here — streaming a response, handling a timeout, rate limiting an endpoint — depends on the call already living behind a server-side route handler. None of it is retrofittable onto a browser calling Claude directly, because the browser has no trustworthy, shared position to do any of it from. Getting the key off the client isn't just a security fix in isolation; it's the prerequisite that makes everything else in this module buildable at all.

A server-side route handler isn't just where the key hides — it's the only position from which validating input, capping cost, and rate limiting are even possible, which is why every later lesson in this module depends on it.

title: A minimal server route that proxies the call
description: Writing a Route Handler that forwards a request to Claude and returns a clean, frontend-friendly response, without leaking internal API shapes or crashing on a malformed request.

learningObjectives.text: Write a Route Handler that validates input before calling Claude
Shape a proxy route's response so the frontend never depends on Anthropic's raw API shape

contentSections.title: The proxy that just forwards everything

contentSections.body: A first-draft `/api/brief` route takes whatever the browser sends, hands it straight to `client.messages.create(req.body)`, and returns `message` untouched. It works for the happy path. It also means the frontend now has to understand Anthropic's exact response shape — `content[0].text`, `stop_reason`, `usage` — and any change to that shape on Anthropic's side breaks briefdesk's UI with no warning.

contentSections.question: This route works today. What's the actual design problem with forwarding the request body directly into messages.create, and the raw response directly back to the browser?

options.label: Nothing — await is used correctly and the route functions as intended

The frontend now has to know Anthropic's exact request and response shape, and the browser can send arbitrary fields (model, max_tokens, system) straight through to the API with no server-side control
This should be a GET request, not POST, since it's just fetching a response

feedback.no-await: The async/await usage is fine mechanically — the problem isn't a bug in this narrow sense, it's what the route's shape lets happen.
feedback.leaky-passthrough: Right. Passing `body` straight into `messages.create` means the browser controls every field Anthropic's API accepts — including `model` (letting a client request an expensive model) and `max_tokens` (letting a client uncap cost) — with nothing server-side deciding what's actually allowed. And returning `message` unmodified means the frontend has to parse Anthropic's exact response shape, coupling briefdesk's UI to an external API's internal structure that can change independent of briefdesk's own release schedule.
feedback.wrong-http-method: POST is the right choice here — the request has a body (the client notes) and triggers an action with a real cost, which is exactly what POST is for. The method isn't the issue.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is a route that defines its own request and response contract, independent of Anthropic's: accept only the specific fields briefdesk actually needs (`clientNotes`), construct the Claude API call itself with `model` and `max_tokens` fixed on the server, and return a shape the frontend defines and controls (`{ brief: string }`), not whatever Anthropic happened to send back.

contentSections.body: A proxy route should define its own request and response shape, validate before calling Claude, and fix model/max_tokens server-side — forwarding the browser's body and Anthropic's response unmodified hands control to the client.

contentSections.title: What the frontend should never see

contentSections.body: Claude returns a rate-limit error. briefdesk's route catches the exception and forwards Anthropic's raw error object straight to the browser — including an internal request ID and a message referencing Anthropic's own account limits. The frontend renders it verbatim: 'anthropic.RateLimitError: Number of request tokens has exceeded...'. A user has no idea what that means or what to do.

contentSections.scenario: briefdesk's route currently does `catch (err) { return Response.json(err); }` — forwarding whatever Anthropic's SDK throws directly to the browser, unmodified, for every failure type.
contentSections.question: What should the route send the browser instead, and where should the raw error detail go?

options.label: Keep forwarding the raw error — it's the most accurate description of what happened
Log the raw error server-side, and send the browser a plain-language message on a status code it can branch on
Catch the error and return a generic 200 OK with empty content, so the UI never has to handle an error state

feedback.raw-forward: Accurate to Anthropic's internals isn't the same as useful to briefdesk's user — a message built for a developer debugging the Anthropic SDK tells a person writing a client brief nothing about what to do next.
feedback.shape-and-log: Right. The raw error is genuinely useful — just not to the browser. Server-side logs are where a developer debugging the issue should find it; the browser needs a plain-language message and a status code it can act on, the same shaping discipline as a success response.
feedback.swallow-silently: This hides the failure entirely — the user has no idea their brief wasn't generated, and might assume it worked. A silent fake success is worse than a clearly shown error.

contentSections.concept: **Errors need the same shaping discipline as success responses: the raw detail goes to server-side logs where it's useful for debugging, and the browser gets a stable, plain-language message on a status code it can branch on — never the provider's raw exception forwarded as-is.**

contentSections.body: Errors need the same shaping as success responses — log the raw provider error server-side, and return the browser a plain, briefdesk-defined error on a status code the frontend can branch on.

title: Streaming a response into the UI as it arrives
description: Streaming Claude's response through a Route Handler using Server-Sent Events, and reading that stream on the client without waiting for the whole response to land.

learningObjectives.text: Implement a streaming Route Handler that forwards Claude's response chunks as they arrive
Read a streamed response on the client and update the UI progressively

contentSections.body: briefdesk's brief-generation call, non-streamed, takes 8 to 14 seconds for a longer set of client notes — Claude reasoning through deliverables, timeline and scope before returning anything. The UI shows nothing for that entire window, then the full brief appears at once. Support gets a message: "is this stuck?"

contentSections.scenario: Two ways to get the same eventual response from Claude: wait for `client.messages.create()` to fully resolve, then send the complete text back in one JSON response — or use `client.messages.stream()` and forward each text chunk to the browser as it's generated, over Server-Sent Events.
contentSections.question: For an 8-to-14-second brief generation, which approach actually changes the total time Claude takes to finish, and which just changes what the user sees while waiting?

options.label: Streaming makes Claude generate the full response faster
Streaming doesn't change total generation time at all — it changes when the user starts seeing output, which is what actually fixes the 'is this stuck?' problem
There's no meaningful difference between the two approaches for a request this length

feedback.streaming-faster: Claude generates tokens at the same underlying rate either way — streaming doesn't change the model's actual throughput. What changes is whether the browser has to wait for every token before seeing any of them.
feedback.streaming-perceived: Right. The 8-to-14-second generation time is unchanged either way — what streaming buys is the first visible words arriving in well under a second, instead of twelve seconds of silence followed by everything at once. That's the entire fix for the 'is this stuck?' report: a user watching text actively appear has no reason to wonder if something's frozen.
feedback.no-difference: The difference is exactly the support complaint — twelve seconds of nothing reads as broken; twelve seconds of visibly arriving text reads as working. Total time is the same; what the user experiences during that time is not.

contentSections.concept: **Streaming doesn't make an AI call faster — it changes a single long silent wait into continuous visible progress, which is what actually reads as "working" instead of "stuck."** The fix for a slow perceived response is very often not making it faster at all — it's making its progress visible.

contentSections.body: Streaming doesn't change how long Claude takes to finish — it changes twelve seconds of silence into twelve seconds of visible progress, which is the entire fix for a response that otherwise reads as frozen.

contentSections.title: Reading the stream on the client

contentSections.body: The route streams correctly — `curl`ing it shows chunks arriving over a couple of seconds. briefdesk's React component still shows nothing until the connection closes, because it's reading the response with `await res.json()`, which by definition waits for the entire body before returning anything.

contentSections.problem: Read a Server-Sent Events stream from /api/brief on the client, appending each chunk of text to a piece of state as it arrives, so the UI updates progressively instead of waiting for res.json().

steps.label: Get a reader from the response body
steps.why: res.body is a ReadableStream — getReader() gives a handle to pull chunks from it manually instead of waiting for the whole thing, which is exactly what res.json() can't do.

steps.label: Loop, reading one chunk at a time
steps.why: Each reader.read() resolves as soon as a chunk arrives from the server — not when the whole stream finishes — which is the mechanism that lets the UI update progressively.

steps.label: Parse each SSE line and update state
steps.why: Each SSE 'data: {...}' line is one small piece of Claude's response — appending it to existing state, rather than replacing state, is what makes the text visibly grow instead of flicker.

faded.problem: Now do the same for a second streaming endpoint, /api/summary, which streams a summary of an already-generated brief back to the client the same way.

blanks.prompt: How do you get a reader capable of pulling chunks from the response body one at a time?
blanks.why: Same mechanism regardless of endpoint — the response body is a ReadableStream, and getReader() is how you consume it incrementally instead of all at once.

blanks.prompt: What condition from reader.read() tells you the stream has ended and you should stop looping?
blanks.why: reader.read() resolves with { done, value } on every call — done becomes true once the server has closed the stream, which is your signal to stop, distinct from any individual chunk's content.

blanks.prompt: Given a decoded chunk of text possibly containing multiple SSE lines, how do you isolate just the actual data payloads?
accept: split on newlines and filter lines starting with 'data: '
blanks.why: A single chunk from the network doesn't necessarily align to exactly one SSE event — splitting and filtering is what correctly separates multiple data: lines that may have arrived together, or handles a data: line split across two chunks if you buffer partial lines.

contentSections.procedure: Reading any SSE stream on the client follows the same shape regardless of what's being streamed: get a reader from res.body, loop reading chunks until done, decode and split each chunk into individual data: lines, and update state incrementally rather than replacing it — the incremental update is what turns a stream of small chunks into text that visibly grows on screen.

contentSections.body: res.json() waits for the entire response body — reading a stream progressively requires res.body.getReader(), a manual read loop, and appending each parsed chunk to state instead of replacing it.

title: Timeouts, retries and a request that never finishes
description: Setting a real timeout on a Claude call so a slow request fails instead of hanging indefinitely, and retrying only the failures where a second attempt has a genuine chance of succeeding.

learningObjectives.text: Set an explicit timeout on a Claude API call rather than relying on a default that may not exist
